source_title: Eleven Power to pursue legal remedies after HERC halts licence process
source_excerpt: Medanta Cofounder Sunil Sachdeva-led Eleven Power Private Ltd (EPPL) has said it will pursue legal remedies in the matter involving the stay by the Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission (HERC) on the process of granting a licence to the company for parallel power distribution in two cities, Gurugram and Nuh. “We hold both the Commission and the state government in the highest regard, and we will continue to engage with them in the same respectful and constructive manner in which we have engaged throughout. We will pursue the remedies available to us under law,” the company said in a statement. On October 19, the Commission allowed EPPL to obtain a parallel distribution licence for 25 years in the two cities, and directed the company to convey its willingness to accept the licence within one week. After receiving EPPL’s acceptance, the Commission was required to publish a public notice. Eleven Power conveyed its acceptance of the distribution licence to the regulator along with the stipulated terms and conditions on October 21. Two days later, EPPL informed HERC that it was taking necessary steps towards implementation of the licence. The company also requested HERC to provide advance intimation and an opportunity of hearing in respect of any proceedings or applications concerning the approval of the licence. Meanwhile, on October 26, the commissioner and secretary to the government of Haryana issued a directive to HERC under Section 108(1) of the Electricity Act, stating that no parallel distribution licence be created or operationalised anywhere in the state. The Act states that in the discharge of its functions, the state commission shall be guided by such directions in matters of policy involving public interest as the state government may give to it in writing. The Haryana government’s letter came on the back of widespread protests by the employees of the government-run power distribution company, the Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam, which has had a monopoly on the power distribution network. The Commission passed an order on October 28 rejecting EPPL’s request for both advance intimation and an opportunity for hearing. HERC cited Section 108(1) and 108(2), which state that the decision of the state government on whether a question relates to a matter of policy involving public interest is final. “The directions dated October 26 have been issued in writing under Section 108(1) and apply generally throughout the State of Haryana. No adjudicatory exercise is left for the Commission to undertake in giving effect to them, and no list is pending before it in which EPPL’s rights are to be determined afresh,” HERC said in its October 28 order. The Commission further stated that in view of the directions issued by the Government of Haryana under Section 108 of the Electricity Act, HERC has decided not to proceed further in the matter for so long as the state government's directions remain operative. The order was passed by Mukesh Garg, Officiating Chairman, and Shiv Kumar, Member, HERC. EPPL said in its statement that Gurugram and Nuh deserve world-class, reliable power and real consumer choice, as Mumbai has had for decades. "Eleven has been part of building Gurugram for many years, and our commitment to its people and to Nuh is unchanged. We will continue to work with all stakeholders in the larger interest of consumers and the state,” it said. The development comes at a time the central government is experimenting with parallel licensing amid muted progress in discom privatisation. Parallel licensing applications across the country have been gaining momentum over the past few months, with Tata Power, Adani Electricity and Torrent Power applying for licensing in areas of Maharashtra, Karnataka, Chhattisgarh and Goa. Andhra Pradesh government has also given Google a deemed distribution licence for its 1 gigawatt artificial intelligence (AI) data centre hub near Visakhapatnam.
